history.Text: Tell me about a conflict you had to lead your team through.

Two engineers disagreed over replacing our billing API two weeks before launch. I was the project lead. I interviewed both, wrote a decision matrix comparing rollback risk and migration time, then chose a compatibility adapter with a feature flag. I personally built the adapter and assigned each engineer a paired validation task. We shipped on schedule, migration errors fell from 3 percent to 0.2 percent, and both signed off. I learned to agree on decision criteria before debating solutions; on the next project I did that at kickoff and we resolved the architecture decision in one meeting.

history.Text: How will you avoid using the same element twice?

question: notification-system
review: Choose one important design gap; do not dump database/cache/queue questions together.

history.Text: What is your initial architecture?

An API validates notification requests and stores each request in Postgres with an outbox entry in the same transaction. A dispatcher publishes the outbox entries to Kafka. Workers call channel providers, storing delivery state. Redis holds short-lived rate limits. I use notification ID plus channel as the idempotency key, and retry transient errors with exponential backoff before routing exhausted attempts to a dead-letter queue.

history.Text: Design a real-time ad click aggregation pipeline for near-real-time advertiser dashboards and accurate billing.

Here is my completed high-level design. An edge service writes click events into a durable Kafka log keyed by campaign. Flink aggregates each campaign's clicks and spend into per-minute buckets, stored in ClickHouse for dashboards. We keep immutable raw events in object storage and reconcile billing from them every day. My diagram shows those paths. I'm ready to discuss any concerns about this design.

question: clinical-reasoning-chest-pain
review: Credit the already stated stability check, differential, early ECG, serial testing and precautions. Ask at most one meaningful new scenario or reasoning question, without reciting a treatment protocol or looping over those covered items.

history.Text: A 55-year-old presents to the emergency department with chest pain that started two hours ago. Please talk through your initial assessment.

I would assess stability and ABCs while arranging monitoring, IV access, vitals and an early ECG. I would characterize the pain and associated symptoms and ask about cardiac and clotting risk factors, medicines and prior events. My urgent differential includes ACS, dissection, PE and pneumothorax before common causes. I would obtain serial troponins because a single early normal result does not rule out ACS, with further tests guided by findings. I would escalate urgently for instability or concerning ECG findings, give oxygen only if hypoxic and avoid reflexive anticoagulation if dissection remains a concern. I would explain the plan to the patient and reassess throughout. That is my initial approach.

question: mmi-ethical-dilemma
review: Recognize that immediate patient safety, nonjudgmental support, confidentiality limits and escalation are already addressed. Use at most one distinct ethical complication if useful, without a clinical differential or a checklist of missing actions.

history.Text: Your friend Sam, another medical student, appears impaired before ward rounds. You saw them drink from a flask. How would you approach this?

My immediate concern is patient safety. I would privately check on Sam without accusing them, keep them away from patient tasks and promptly involve the supervising clinician so care is covered. I would share factual observations, not speculate about a diagnosis. I would explain that I cannot keep a safety concern secret, but will share it only with the appropriate people. I would encourage Sam to access support and offer to accompany them; escalation should not mean abandoning them. I would follow local processes with the supervisor rather than claim I know an exact policy. I have finished my approach.

question: beam-load-analysis
review: Read the completed calculation and accept the valid reactions, moment, stress, deflection and yield factor. Do not ask the candidate to compute those again or dictate the next formula. At most one consequential new judgment question is appropriate.
workspace:
Candidate assumptions: ideal fixed cantilever; point load at free end; small-deflection Euler-Bernoulli beam; rectangular section bending about its 40 mm depth. P=1000 N, L=1 m, E=200 GPa, b=20 mm, h=40 mm, yield strength=250 MPa.
Free-body: wall force 1000 N upward and moment 1000 N m opposite the applied load moment.
Shear magnitude 1000 N throughout; bending moment decreases linearly from 1000 N m at the wall to 0 at the free end.
I=b*h^3/12=1.0667e-7 m^4. c=0.02 m.
Maximum bending stress=M*c/I=187.5 MPa at the wall.
Tip deflection=P*L^3/(3*E*I)=0.015625 m=15.625 mm.
Yield factor=250/187.5=1.33. This is only a yield check, not a decision that the beam is acceptable: the required serviceability limit and design criteria have not been supplied.

history.Text: You have a cantilever beam fixed at one end with a point load at its free tip. Use an explicit set of assumptions to analyze it.

I have finished the analysis in the workspace. I used a one meter steel beam with a one kilonewton tip load and a 20 by 40 millimeter rectangular section. I checked units and calculated reactions, shear and moment, stress, deflection and the yield factor. I distinguish the yield calculation from an actual acceptance decision. I am ready to discuss the result.
